analogy.p: A fermenter is like a brewery or a bread-maker: you give living yeast-like cells food, warmth and air, keep out intruders, and collect what they grow. A GM crop is like editing one line of a recipe so that every loaf made from it has the new feature. The analogy breaks down because a gene change in a crop is permanent and passed on to its seeds, and a living crop interacts with the wider environment, unlike a sealed brewery.
analogy.t: A brewery for protein, and a recipe edit for crops

bullets: Two spec ideas here: growing a fungus for **mycoprotein**, and **genetically modified (GM) crops**.
Both aim to produce more food from less land, which is important when the human population is rising.
Microorganisms reproduce rapidly, so biomass builds up quickly.
Production in tanks is independent of climate, soil quality and the seasons.
Biotechnology often needs high start-up costs and energy, so you must weigh benefits against costs.
Link: genetic engineering, respiration, aerobic conditions, trophic levels and biodiversity.
core.p: **Biotechnology** is the use of living organisms, or parts of them, to make useful products. In food production, modern biotechnological techniques have enabled large quantities of microorganism biomass to be produced for human consumption. This links directly to **food security**, which is having enough food to feed a population, because microorganisms grow fast, need little land and are not affected by the weather when grown in a controlled tank.

bullets: Fusarium is a **fungus**, not a plant or bacterium.
Mycoprotein is high in protein and is used as a meat substitute for vegetarians.
It is made from the **biomass** of the fungus (the living material that has grown).
The fungus is grown in large vessels called **fermenters** (also called bioreactors).
Mycoprotein can be produced all year round and does not need farmland or animals.
Link: protein is needed for growth and repair; this gives a non-animal source of it.
core.p: **Mycoprotein** is a protein-rich food made from the biomass of the fungus Fusarium. It is suitable for vegetarians because no animal is involved in its production. A fungus is made of thread-like hyphae that form a mass called a mycelium; when this biomass is harvested, purified and processed it can be shaped into meat-substitute foods. The fungus is grown on glucose syrup in aerobic conditions, and the biomass is harvested and purified before being eaten.

bullets: **Glucose syrup**: food (energy source and raw material) for the fungus.
**Oxygen** (sterile air): needed for aerobic respiration, which releases the most energy for growth.
**Optimum temperature**: enzymes work fastest; too cold means slow growth and too hot denatures enzymes.
**Optimum pH**: enzymes also have an optimum pH; extremes denature them.
**Nutrients and minerals** (a source of nitrogen etc.) to make proteins.
No light is needed because the fungus does not photosynthesise.
core.h: What the fungus needs to grow
core.p: Like all living organisms, the fungus needs the right conditions to grow quickly. It is grown on **glucose syrup**, which provides the energy source for respiration and the carbon for building new cells (proteins, carbohydrates and so on). Because the fungus respires aerobically, it needs a constant supply of oxygen. Other nutrients and minerals are added for making proteins, along with a suitable temperature and pH so that the enzymes inside the fungus work at their optimum.

bullets: **Sterile conditions**: prevents contamination by other microorganisms that would compete for glucose or spoil the product.
**Stirrer / paddles**: mix the contents so nutrients, oxygen and heat are evenly distributed.
**Air supply**: oxygen bubbled in at the bottom for aerobic respiration.
**Water jacket**: cooling water takes away the heat released by respiration, keeping the temperature at the optimum.
**Probes and sensors** monitor pH and temperature so conditions can be adjusted automatically.
**Harvesting**: some of the culture is removed so the biomass can be separated and purified, and fresh nutrients are added.
core.h: The fermenter: design and how it works
core.p: A fermenter is a large vessel in which microorganisms are grown under controlled conditions. It is first **sterilised** so that no unwanted microorganisms compete with the fungus or contaminate the product. Glucose syrup and nutrients are added, sterile air is bubbled in, and a motor-driven stirrer keeps everything mixed. Probes monitor the temperature and pH, and a water jacket (cooling) removes the heat released by respiration so the fungus does not get too hot.

bullets: Aseptic (sterile) conditions: stops competition from other microbes, so more glucose goes to the fungus and the product is safe.
Temperature control: keeps enzymes working at their optimum rate; too high denatures them.
pH control: maintains the optimum for enzymes.
Oxygen supply: allows aerobic respiration, giving energy for rapid growth.
Stirring: spreads oxygen, nutrients and heat evenly and stops local shortages.
Removing product: avoids a build-up of waste products and lets production continue.
core.h: Why these control features matter (explain, do not just list)
core.p: Exam questions reward linking each feature to its purpose. Every control is there to keep conditions at the optimum for enzymes and growth, or to protect the product. For example, respiration releases energy and some of it is released as heat, so without a cooling jacket the contents would overheat and enzymes would denature. Without stirring, the fungus near the bottom would run out of oxygen and glucose.

bullets: Fewer energy-transfer steps than feeding crops to animals, so less is lost.
High growth rate: biomass can double in a matter of hours.
Needs far less land and water than farming cattle for the same mass of protein.
Production is not affected by drought, floods or seasons.
The glucose can come from cheap sources such as waste starch, though this should be stated as an example, not a requirement.
Mycoprotein supports food security by providing protein without needing farmland.
core.h: Why mycoprotein is a sustainable use of resources
core.p: Producing protein from a fungus is more efficient than producing meat because there is no animal in the chain. In a food chain only about 10% of biomass is passed on at each trophic level, so converting plant material to meat loses a great deal. A fermenter turns glucose directly into fungal protein, and the fungus doubles its biomass quickly, so a lot of food can be made in a small area in a short time.

bullets: Advantages: protein-rich, suitable for vegetarians, fast production, low land use, all-year-round, low risk of weather damage.
Disadvantages: expensive equipment, energy needed to sterilise, heat and aerate; skilled operators needed.
Contamination can ruin a whole batch, so strict control is essential.
Some people may have an allergic reaction or dislike the texture and flavour; the product usually needs flavouring.
Use data (e.g. protein per 100 g, cost per kg) to support your comparison with meat.
Sustainability depends on where the glucose and energy come from.
core.p: Examiners can ask you to evaluate the use of microorganisms in food production using data or information given. Weigh up advantages such as high protein content and sustainability against disadvantages such as high start-up costs, the energy needed for sterile conditions, and the fact that some people dislike the taste or texture or have an allergic reaction to it. Always finish with a judgement that follows from your points.

bullets: Genes are sections of DNA that code for proteins, so a gene for a useful protein can give a new characteristic.
**Restriction enzymes** cut the required gene from the DNA of the donor organism.
The gene is inserted into a **vector**, usually a bacterial **plasmid** or a virus, using **ligase** enzyme to join the DNA (Higher tier detail on enzymes).
The vector is used to insert the gene into the required cells of the crop plant.
Transferring genes at an early stage means every cell of the mature plant carries the new gene.
Link: genetic engineering is also used to make human insulin in GM bacteria, and in medicine.
core.h: Genetic engineering: the principle behind GM crops
core.p: In **genetic engineering**, genes from the chromosomes of one organism can be 'cut out' and transferred to the cells of another organism, using enzymes. The organism that receives the new gene is called genetically modified (GM). The transfer is carried out at an early stage of development (for example in plant cells, a seed or an embryo) so that the organism develops with the desired characteristic. Plants that have had their genes modified in this way are called GM crops.

bullets: **Insect-resistant crops** (e.g. Bt maize or cotton with a bacterial gene): less damage by pests, so a higher yield and less insecticide needed.
**Herbicide-resistant crops**: farmers can spray herbicide to kill weeds without harming the crop.
**Disease-resistant crops**: lower losses to pathogens.
**Bigger or better fruits**, higher yield or improved nutritional value (e.g. golden rice, engineered to make a vitamin A precursor).
**Crops that tolerate poor conditions**, for example drought or salty soil, can be grown in more places.
The extra yield helps feed a growing population.
core.p: Crops have been genetically engineered for several useful characteristics. These include resistance to insect attack or to herbicides, resistance to disease, and increased yield or improved nutritional content. GM crops therefore help raise the yield of the farmed land, which supports food security, and can reduce losses to pests, which links directly to the threats to food security.

bullets: Selective breeding: choose and breed the best individuals over many generations; limited to genes already in the species.
Genetic engineering: a specific gene is transferred in one generation, even from a different species.
GE is faster and more targeted; selective breeding is slower but more widely accepted.
Both reduce genetic variation if only a few varieties are used, which can increase vulnerability to disease.
Both can raise food production and so support food security.
Examiners may ask for one similarity and one difference: give both clearly.
core.p: Both approaches produce organisms with desired characteristics, but they work differently. Selective breeding chooses parents with the best characteristics from the existing variation and takes many generations over several years. Genetic engineering moves a specific gene directly, often between unrelated species, in a single step. This makes it faster and more precise, but it also raises more concerns for some people.

bullets: **Health**: some people worry that eating GM food may harm health; scientific testing is carried out to check safety.
**Environment**: possible effects on populations of wild flowers and insects, and on food webs.
Genes could spread (by pollen) to wild plants or to non-GM crops.
Herbicide-resistant crops can encourage heavy herbicide use, and weeds may evolve resistance.
**Economic**: GM seed can be expensive, which can disadvantage poorer farmers.
Ethical views differ, so use balanced language rather than claiming the technology is simply good or bad.
core.p: Not everyone agrees that GM crops are a good idea. Some people feel that eating GM crops may be harmful to human health, although the evidence so far does not show this and the full long-term effects are still debated. There are also concerns about the effect on populations of wild flowers and insects, for example if genes spread to wild relatives or if insects that are not pests are harmed. Economic and ethical concerns also exist.

bullets: Both can help feed a growing population (rising birth rate).
GM crops tackle new pests and pathogens, and changing environment, by building in resistance or tolerance.
Mycoprotein reduces dependence on animal farming, which loses energy at each trophic level.
Costs: fermenters and GM research are expensive and need regulation.
Public acceptance affects whether a new food is used.
Always link back to the definition: food security means having enough food to feed a population.
core.h: Mycoprotein and GM crops together: food security
core.p: Both technologies address the threats to food security by increasing the amount of food produced from limited resources. Mycoprotein adds an extra protein source made in fermenters without needing land, while GM crops raise yields and protect against pests and poor conditions. Neither is a complete solution, and each has costs and risks, so evaluation questions expect you to compare them.

bullets: Percentage change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100.
For exponential-looking growth, give how long it takes to double and use it to predict.
Comment on whether the data is enough: sample size, repeats, and who collected it (bias).
State a judgement and justify it using the data and the benefits and risks.
Use command words: 'describe' = what happens; 'explain' = why; 'evaluate' = weigh up and conclude.
Link to other topics: respiration, enzymes and denaturation, natural selection (resistance), food chains.
core.h: Interpreting data and answering evaluation questions
core.p: You may be given tables or graphs, for example yields of GM and non-GM crops, or the growth of fungal biomass over time, and asked to interpret them. Read the axes and units, describe the pattern with figures, and use the data in your explanation. For a 6 mark evaluation, give both sides with biological reasoning and end with a justified conclusion.

exam: State what mycoprotein is: 'a protein-rich food made from the fungus Fusarium, suitable for vegetarians' (1 to 2 marks).
Conditions: grown on glucose syrup in aerobic conditions; always say why (oxygen for aerobic respiration, glucose for energy and growth).
Fermenter feature questions: name the feature AND its purpose, for example 'water jacket to remove heat from respiration so enzymes are not denatured'.
'Explain why the fermenter must be sterile' = to prevent contamination by other microorganisms that compete for nutrients or spoil the product.
Genetic engineering: describe in order: gene isolated with enzymes, inserted into a vector (plasmid or virus), vector transfers it into crop cells at an early stage.
Give examples of GM crops: insect-resistant, herbicide-resistant, higher-yielding or better nutrition.
For concerns, use the spec ideas: effect on human health and effect on populations of wild flowers and insects.
6-mark evaluation: at least two benefits, two concerns, link to food security, and a clear justified conclusion.
Calculation tips: percentage increase = change ÷ original × 100; give units (t/ha, kg) and show working.
Graph tips: read axes, quote two values, state the trend (e.g. doubling every 5 hours) and use it to predict.
Avoid 'GM is bad' or 'GM is good' alone: use 'could', 'may', and give reasons.

mistakes.w: Fusarium is a bacterium (or a plant).

mistakes.r: It is fed glucose syrup and respires aerobically; no light is needed.
mistakes.w: The fungus makes the protein using photosynthesis.

mistakes.r: Sterile conditions stop contamination by other microorganisms that would compete for nutrients or spoil the product.
mistakes.w: The fermenter is kept sterile so the fungus is not killed.

mistakes.r: It removes the heat released by respiration to keep the temperature at the optimum.
mistakes.w: The water jacket keeps the fungus warm.

mistakes.r: That is selective breeding. GM crops have a gene transferred using enzymes and a vector.
mistakes.w: GM crops are made by breeding the best plants together.

mistakes.r: The gene is inserted at an early stage so all the plant's cells have the new gene.
mistakes.w: Genetic engineering changes the plant after it has grown.

mistakes.r: Say that some people are concerned about health and effects on wild flowers and insects, and weigh these against benefits like higher yield.
mistakes.w: GM crops are definitely unsafe (or definitely safe).

mistakes.r: It is made from fungal biomass and is suitable for vegetarians.

summary: AQA Biology only (4.7.3.4 food security and genetic engineering links): you must know how the fungus Fusarium is grown in aerobic fermenters on glucose syrup to make mycoprotein, a protein-rich food suitable for vegetarians, and how GM crops are produced and used (e.g. insect-resistant, herbicide-resistant and higher-yielding crops), and be able to evaluate both. It matters because it shows how biotechnology can increase food supply sustainably, and exams ask you to interpret data and weigh up benefits against concerns.

terms.d: The use of living organisms or their parts to produce useful products or processes.
A protein-rich food, suitable for vegetarians, made from the biomass of the fungus Fusarium.
A fungus grown in fermenters to produce mycoprotein.
A large vessel in which microorganisms are grown under controlled conditions.
Needing or using oxygen, as in aerobic respiration.
A concentrated sugar solution used as the energy and carbon source for the fungus.
Transferring a gene from the chromosomes of one organism into the cells of another using enzymes, to give a desired characteristic.
A crop plant that has had its genes altered by genetic engineering.
A carrier, usually a bacterial plasmid or a virus, used to insert a gene into the required cells.
A small ring of DNA in bacteria that can be used as a vector.
An enzyme that cuts DNA at specific sequences, used to isolate a required gene.
An enzyme that joins pieces of DNA together.
Choosing parents with desired characteristics to breed over many generations.
Having enough food to feed a population.

worked.q: In a trial, non-GM maize gave a yield of 6.0 tonnes per hectare and insect-resistant GM maize gave 7.5 tonnes per hectare. Calculate the percentage increase in yield. (2 marks)
A fermenter contains 2 kg of fungal biomass. The biomass doubles every 5 hours. Calculate the biomass after 20 hours. (2 marks)

worked.ans: GM crops, produced by transferring a useful gene using enzymes and a vector into crop cells, can have a higher yield or resist insects, so more food is produced from the same land and less is lost to pests, which supports food security for a growing population. However, some people are concerned that eating them may harm health, and genes or herbicide use could affect wild flowers and insects, and the seed may be expensive for poorer farmers. Overall, if rigorous testing shows they are safe and they are managed to protect wild species, the benefits for food supply are likely to outweigh the risks.
worked.q: Evaluate the use of genetically modified crops to increase food security. (6 marks)
steps: Say what GM crops are: genes transferred into crop cells so they have characteristics such as insect resistance, herbicide tolerance or higher yield.
Benefits: higher yield per hectare, less crop lost to pests so more food, less pesticide, can grow in poorer conditions; this helps feed a rising population.
Concerns: some people fear harm to health; possible effect on populations of wild flowers and insects; costly seed and long-term effects are uncertain.
Compare: GM is faster than selective breeding but more controversial.
Judgement: weigh these up and justify.
